title: Chapter XXIX

teacherSummary.text: At Rosings, Lady Catherine dominates the conversation, questions Elizabeth about her family and education, and is surprised when Elizabeth answers boldly and will not state her age.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXIX,” how does Austen show an imperious hostess? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXIX develops the idea of an imperious hostess. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XXIX to complicate the reader's understanding of an imperious hostess. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXIX within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of an imperious hostess responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXIX as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of an imperious hostess. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

annotationFocus.label: Characterization

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: What does Elizabeth's refusal to state her age show? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include cassino, glazing, conciliating, dictating, overpower. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “Collins sat down to quadrille; and as Miss de Bourgh chose to play at cassino, the two girls had the honour of assisting Mrs.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: A game at cards, played by two or more persons, usually for twenty-one points.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Aristocrats expected deference; governesses and accomplishments signaled status. Now, why does this chapter matter? Elizabeth's independence before rank sets up her later confrontation with Lady Catherine. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Irony, Setting.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot characterization, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.

segments.activity: One-sentence claim plus one quoted piece of evidence.
segments.script: To close: in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about an imperious hostess, and back it with one short quotation. Hand it to me on your way out.
